\title{Hess's Law}
\summary{In this lab we decompose Baking Soda by heating it. Then we use Hess's Law and two reactions that we can measure the heat of to find the heat of decomposition.}
\tags{Hess's law, thermochemistry, calorimetry, enthalpy}
\minutes{70}

In this lab you will find the enthalpy change (ΔH) of a reaction you cannot measure directly: baking soda breaking down when it is heated. You will run that reaction in a pan to see what it produces, and then run two different reactions in a foam-cup calorimeter that you *can* measure. Hess's law lets you combine the results of those two measured reactions to calculate ΔH of the one you couldn't measure.

Target reaction (cannot be measured directly):

$$\ce{2 NaHCO3(s) -> Na2CO3(s) + H2O(g) + CO2(g)} \qquad \Delta H = ?$$

| | Reaction | How ΔH is obtained |
|---|---|---|
| A | $\ce{NaHCO3(s) + H+(aq) -> Na+(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)}$ | Measured (Cup A) |
| B | $\ce{Na2CO3(s) + 2 H+(aq) -> 2 Na+(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)}$ | Measured (Cup B) |
| C | $\ce{H2O(l) -> H2O(g)}$ | Given: $\pu{+44.0 kJ/mol}$ |

\info{
Reactions A and B produce liquid water at room temperature; reaction C converts it to the water vapor that actually leaves the pan.
}

Before beginning, use Hess's law to determine how reactions A, B, and C combine to give the target reaction. Every species other than those in the target must cancel. Write the combination and the resulting expression for $\Delta H_{\text{target}}$ in terms of $\Delta H_A$, $\Delta H_B$, and $\Delta H_C$.

\answer[id=hess-derivation, lines=6]{Combination of A, B, and C that yields the target reaction, and the expression for $\Delta H_{\text{target}}$.}

# Materials

**Chemicals**

- [ ] Sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), approximately 6 g
- [ ] Citric acid powder, 12 g
- [ ] Distilled water, 60 mL

**Equipment**

- [ ] Two foam cups, nested
- [ ] Thermometer reading to 0.1 °C
- [ ] Scale reading to 0.01 g (0.1 g acceptable with reduced precision)
- [ ] Small dry skillet or saucepan and a stove (a foil tray may be used in place of the skillet; see Part 1)
- [ ] A drinking glass chilled in the refrigerator or freezer
- [ ] Beaker for the acid solution, metal spoon, match or lighter, graduated cylinder, safety goggles

# Safety

\safety{
Wear safety goggles throughout. The pan in Part 1 reaches approximately 200 °C: handle it only by the handle, keep the exterior dry, and allow it to cool before weighing. Citric acid solution is a mild irritant; rinse any skin contact with water, and rinse eye contact for 15 minutes. The reactions in Part 2 release $\ce{CO2}$ gas. No materials in this experiment are flammable.
}

# Preparation

**0.1**  Weigh **12 g** of citric acid powder and add it to **60 mL** of distilled water in a beaker. Stir until fully dissolved. Dissolving citric acid cools the water, so prepare this solution first and let it stand until it returns to room temperature (about 15 minutes) before Part 2. Label it **1 M citric acid**.

\notes[id=notes-prep]{Notes on preparation}

# Part 1 — Thermal decomposition of sodium bicarbonate

**1.1**  Weigh **4.00 g** of sodium bicarbonate to 0.01 g and record as $m_{\text{start}}$: \input[id=m-start, unit=g]. Weigh the empty, dry pan and record as $m_{\text{pan}}$: \input[id=m-pan, unit=g]. Transfer the sample to the pan and spread it into a thin layer.

**1.2**  Heat the pan on medium. Water vapor and $\ce{CO2}$ are released as the solid decomposes.

**1.3**  Stir occasionally. After approximately 5 minutes, when no further vapor is released, remove the pan from the heat, allow it to cool for 5 minutes, and weigh the pan with residue. Reheat for 2 minutes, cool, and weigh again. Repeat until two consecutive weighings agree within 0.02 g. Record the final value as $m_{\text{pan+residue}}$: \input[id=m-pan-residue, unit=g]

**1.4**  Calculate the residue mass. For complete conversion of $\ce{NaHCO3}$ ($\pu{84.01 g/mol}$) to $\ce{Na2CO3}$ ($\pu{105.99 g/mol}$), the expected residue mass is $m_{\text{start}} \times 105.99 / (2 \times 84.01) = 0.631 \times m_{\text{start}}$, approximately 2.52 g. Record the ratio of measured to expected residue mass: \input[id=residue-ratio]. Retain the residue for Part 2, Cup B.

\tip[label="Note on step 1.1"]{
A sheet of aluminum foil folded into a shallow tray with raised edges can be used instead of a skillet. Weigh the empty tray as $m_{\text{pan}}$ and set it directly on the burner. Handle it with tongs; it heats and cools quickly. Because the foil is light, weighing the residue is easier than with a heavy pan.
}

\tip[label="Note on step 1.2"]{
The products can be confirmed during heating. Holding a chilled glass inverted about 10 cm above the pan produces condensation from the water vapor, and a lit match lowered to just above the solid is extinguished by the $\ce{CO2}$ accumulating in the pan.
}

\notes[id=notes-part1]{Notes on Part 1}

# Part 2 — Calorimetry

### Calorimeter setup

**2.1**  Nest two foam cups and weigh them. Add approximately **25 mL** of the citric acid solution to the inner cup and weigh again. Record the mass of solution as $m_{\text{acid}}$ to 0.01 g.

**2.2**  Insert the thermometer so the bulb is in the liquid but not touching the bottom, and wait 1 minute. Record the steady temperature as $T_{\text{initial}}$.

### Cup A — sodium bicarbonate

**2.3**  Weigh **2.00 g** of fresh sodium bicarbonate (not the residue) to 0.01 g and record as $m_A$: \input[id=m-a, unit=g]

**2.4**  Start a timer. Add the solid in small portions over approximately 1 minute to control foaming. Transfer the entire sample.

**2.5**  Swirl gently and continuously, reading the thermometer every 15 s. The temperature decreases. Record the lowest temperature reached as $T_{\text{min},A}$: \input[id=t-min-a, unit=°C]. Continue reading for 1 minute past the minimum to confirm it.

### Cup B — decomposition residue from Part 1

**2.6**  Rinse and dry the inner cup. Repeat steps 2.1–2.2 with fresh acid solution and record the new $m_{\text{acid}}$ and $T_{\text{initial}}$.

**2.7**  Weigh **1.50 g** of the Part 1 residue to 0.01 g and record the actual mass as $m_B$: \input[id=m-b, unit=g]

**2.8**  Add the solid in small portions over approximately 1 minute, swirling continuously. The temperature increases. Record the highest temperature reached as $T_{\text{max},B}$: \input[id=t-max-b, unit=°C]

\notes[id=notes-part2]{Notes on Part 2}

Determine $\Delta H_A$ and $\Delta H_B$ in kJ/mol from the calorimetry data, then apply the expression for $\Delta H_{\text{target}}$ you derived at the start of the lab. Compare the result to the accepted value of $\pu{+135.6 kJ}$ per 2 mol $\ce{NaHCO3}$ and compute the percent error. As a final calculation, determine the energy in joules required to fully decompose one teaspoon (approximately 4.6 g) of sodium bicarbonate.

\answer[id=calc-dh, lines=8]{Show your calculation of $\Delta H_A$, $\Delta H_B$, and $\Delta H_{\text{target}}$.}

\answer[id=calc-error, lines=3]{Percent error compared to $\pu{+135.6 kJ}$.}

\answer[id=calc-teaspoon, lines=3]{Energy required to decompose one teaspoon (4.6 g) of sodium bicarbonate.}

# Data table

\datatable[id=data, title="Data table"]{
| Quantity | Part 1 | Cup A | Cup B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mass of $\ce{NaHCO3}$ (g) | ___ | ___ | — |
| Mass of pan / pan + residue (g) | ___ | — | — |
| Mass of residue used (g) | — | — | ___ |
| Mass of acid solution (g) | — | ___ | ___ |
| $T_{\text{initial}}$ (°C) | — | ___ | ___ |
| $T_{\text{min}}$ or $T_{\text{max}}$ (°C) | — | ___ | ___ |
| ΔT (°C) | — | ___ | ___ |
| $q_{\text{rxn}}$ (J) | — | ___ | ___ |
| ΔH (kJ/mol) | — | ___ | ___ |
}

\title{Freezing-Point Depression and the van't Hoff Factor}
\summary{Freeze sugar, table salt, and Epsom salt solutions in an ice and salt bath and work out how many particles each solute really splits into.}
\tags{colligative properties, freezing point, van't Hoff factor, solutions}
\minutes{90}

Anything dissolved in water lowers its freezing point, and how much it lowers it depends on how many separate particles the solute breaks into. That count, per formula unit, is the van't Hoff factor, i. In this lab you will measure it for three compounds from the kitchen and pharmacy: sugar, table salt, and Epsom salt. You will dissolve a weighed amount of each in water, freeze a small sample in a jar sitting in an ice and salt bath, then lift it out and watch it melt. The temperature at which the last ice disappears is the freezing point. How far each solution freezes below pure water is the freezing-point depression, and from it you get i.

\info[label="Background (optional)"]{
At the freezing point, ice and liquid water are in balance: water molecules leave the ice surface exactly as fast as they land on it. Dissolving something in the liquid dilutes the water, so fewer water molecules land on the ice each second. Nothing has changed on the ice side, so the ice loses molecules faster than it gains them. Cooling slows the leaving rate more than it slows the landing rate, and at a low enough temperature the two match again. That temperature is the freezing point of the solution. In dilute solutions the size of the temperature drop depends only on how many particles are dissolved, not what they are, which is why properties like this are called colligative. At higher concentrations the particles start to interact with each other and with the water around them, and the simple picture drifts by a measurable amount. One goal of this lab is to show that drift. The solutions are concentrated enough that, for at least one of the three solutes, the van't Hoff factor you measure will sit well below the number of ions a formula unit contains, and the gap is real, not experimental error.
}

# Equations

$$\Delta T_{f} = T_{f,\mathrm{water}} - T_{f,\mathrm{solution}}$$

where $\Delta T_{f}$ is the freezing-point depression, in °C; $T_{f,\mathrm{water}}$ is the freezing point of the water you used, measured with your thermometer, in °C; and $T_{f,\mathrm{solution}}$ is the measured freezing point of the solution, in °C.

$$\Delta T_{f} = i\,K_{f}\,m$$

where $i$ is the van't Hoff factor, with no unit; $K_{f}$ is the freezing-point depression constant of water, 1.86 °C·kg/mol; and $m$ is the molality of the solution, in mol/kg.

$$m = \frac{n}{w}$$

where $m$ is the molality, in mol/kg; $n$ is the amount of solute formula units dissolved, in mol; and $w$ is the total mass of water in the solution, in kg.

# Materials

**Chemicals**

- [ ] Granulated sugar (sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁), about 20 g
- [ ] Non-iodized table salt (sodium chloride, NaCl), about 5 g, for the salt solution. Canning and pickling salt is the same product.
- [ ] Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate heptahydrate, MgSO₄·7H₂O), plain and unscented, about 15 g
- [ ] Water, distilled or tap, about 1 L. The level of impurity does not matter for this lab. The minerals in tap water lower its freezing point by less than the thermometer can read, and the water blank cancels that shift anyway. Use the same water for the blank and for all three solutions.
- [ ] Table salt, any kind, about 300 g, for the cooling bath
- [ ] Ice, about 1 kg

**Equipment**

- [ ] Digital thermometer reading to 0.1 °C, with a metal stem and a range down to at least −20 °C
- [ ] Scale reading to 0.01 g
- [ ] Small glass jar, about 50 mL, for the sample. A spice jar or baby-food jar works. A test tube works just as well if you have one; fill it to the same depth.
- [ ] Beaker, 250 mL or larger, for the cooling bath
- [ ] Three small jars with lids, about 100 mL each
- [ ] Mug, for the ice-point check
- [ ] Teaspoon
- [ ] Paper towels
- [ ] Timer or phone stopwatch
- [ ] Marker or labels

# Safety

\safety{
The ice and salt bath reaches about −15 °C and can cause cold burns with prolonged skin contact. Handle the sample jar by its rim, and do not hold your hand in the bath. Do not taste the solutions; Epsom salt is a laxative.
}

# Preparation

**0.1** Label the three jars "Sucrose", "Table salt", and "Epsom salt".

**0.2** Place the Sucrose jar on the scale and tare it. Add water until the scale reads about **50 g**. The exact amount does not matter; the molality comes from the masses you record. Record the **mass of water** to 0.01 g.

**0.3** Tare the scale with the Sucrose jar and its water on it. Add about **17 g** of sugar. Record the **mass of solute** to 0.01 g.

**0.4** Weigh about **50 g** of water into the Table salt jar as in step 0.2 and record the **mass of water** to 0.01 g. Tare, add about **3 g** of table salt, and record the **mass of solute** to 0.01 g.

**0.5** Weigh about **50 g** of water into the Epsom salt jar as in step 0.2 and record the **mass of water** to 0.01 g. Tare, add about **14 g** of Epsom salt, and record the **mass of solute** to 0.01 g.

**0.6** Cap the three jars and swirl each one until no solid remains. The sugar takes a few minutes of patience. Keep the jars capped from now on except while pouring, to limit evaporation.

**0.7** Fill the mug about half full with ice and add water until the ice is just covered. Stir with the teaspoon for 30 s. The mug must be mostly ice, with only enough water to fill the gaps.

**0.8** Place the thermometer in the ice water with its tip in the middle of the ice, not touching the mug. Stir gently with the thermometer and wait until the reading has not changed for 30 s. Record the **ice-point reading** to 0.1 °C: \input[id=icepoint, unit=°C]
This is what the thermometer reads at a true 0.0 °C. Inexpensive thermometers are often off by a few tenths of a degree, and that is fine. If the reading is more than 1.0 °C from zero, or will not settle, use a different thermometer.

**0.9** Fill the beaker with ice cubes, adding table salt as you go, about one part salt to four parts ice by volume. Add cold tap water until the mixture is a slush. Stir with the teaspoon for 1 minute.

**0.10** Place the thermometer in the bath and wait until the reading has not changed by more than 0.2 °C for 30 s. The bath must read **−8.0 °C** or colder; if it does not, add more salt and stir. Record the bath temperature to 0.1 °C: \input[id=bath, unit=°C]

**0.11** Rinse the thermometer with water and dry it with a paper towel.

# Part 1 — Water

**1.1** Rinse the sample jar and thermometer with water and dry them with a paper towel.

**1.2** Pour fresh water into the clean sample jar to a depth of about **2 cm** (about 15 mL). Place the thermometer in the liquid with its tip in the middle, about 1 cm above the bottom and away from the side of the jar.

**1.3** Push the sample jar down into the bath until the ice and brine come up to about the level of the liquid inside, and pack ice around it so it stays put. The rim of the jar must stay well above the bath so no brine gets in.

**1.4** Stir gently and continuously by moving the thermometer in small circles, keeping its tip in the middle of the liquid, and watch the reading fall. The sample cools below its freezing point without freezing. Then ice appears all at once and the reading jumps up by a degree or more within a few seconds. If the reading reaches −8.0 °C and there is still no ice, touch the corner of an ice cube to the surface of the liquid for about 1 s and take it away.

**1.5** As soon as the reading jumps, lift the jar out of the bath and hold it in the air. Keep swirling the thermometer through the slush. The reading rises slowly as the ice melts. If the jar holds only a trace of ice, put it back in the bath for 20 s and lift it out again.

**1.6** When only a few small pieces of ice are left, slow down. Swirl just enough to keep the liquid mixed and watch the ice. The **freezing point** is the reading at the moment the last piece of ice disappears. Record the **freezing point** to 0.1 °C in the Water row, Trial 1.

**1.7** Set the jar back in the bath as in step 1.3 and follow steps 1.4 through 1.6 again for Trial 2.

**1.8** Empty the jar.

# Part 2 — Sucrose

This part repeats the Part 1 procedure with the sucrose solution in place of plain water.

**2.1** Rinse the sample jar and thermometer with water, then with about 5 mL of sucrose solution, and discard the rinse.

**2.2** Pour sucrose solution into the clean sample jar to a depth of about **2 cm** (about 15 mL). Place the thermometer in the liquid with its tip in the middle, about 1 cm above the bottom and away from the side of the jar.

**2.3** Push the sample jar down into the bath until the ice and brine come up to about the level of the liquid inside, and pack ice around it so it stays put. The rim of the jar must stay well above the bath so no brine gets in.

**2.4** Stir gently and continuously by moving the thermometer in small circles, keeping its tip in the middle of the liquid, and watch the reading fall. The sample cools below its freezing point without freezing. Then ice appears all at once and the reading jumps up by a degree or more within a few seconds. If the reading reaches −8.0 °C and there is still no ice, touch the corner of an ice cube to the surface of the liquid for about 1 s and take it away.

**2.5** As soon as the reading jumps, lift the jar out of the bath and hold it in the air. Keep swirling the thermometer through the slush. The reading rises slowly as the ice melts. If the jar holds only a trace of ice, put it back in the bath for 20 s and lift it out again.

**2.6** When only a few small pieces of ice are left, slow down. Swirl just enough to keep the liquid mixed and watch the ice. The **freezing point** is the reading at the moment the last piece of ice disappears. Record the **freezing point** to 0.1 °C in the Sucrose row, Trial 1.

**2.7** Set the jar back in the bath as in step 2.3 and follow steps 2.4 through 2.6 again for Trial 2.

**2.8** Empty the jar.

The obvious way to read the freezing point, taking the highest reading just after the jump, gives a number that is too low, and the reason is worth understanding. A supercooled sample freezes a burst of ice the moment freezing starts, and ice keeps forming on the cold jar wall for as long as the jar is in the bath. All of that ice is pure water. The liquid left behind holds the same solute in less water, so it is more concentrated than the solution you weighed out, and its freezing point is lower. The thermometer reports the freezing point of that stronger liquid.

Melting undoes this. As the ice melts in the air, the pure water goes back into the liquid, and the solution dilutes back toward its original composition. At the instant the last piece of ice disappears, the liquid is exactly the solution you made, and the temperature is its freezing point. It does not matter how much ice formed or how far the sample supercooled; the end point is the same. An offset in the thermometer does not matter either, because the water and the solutions are read with the same thermometer and the offset cancels when the two are subtracted. What is left is the thermometer lagging a little behind a warming sample, which is why the last few pieces of ice are melted slowly.

\figure[caption="Temperature of a 1 mol/kg table salt sample: cooled in the bath, supercooled, frozen in a burst, held in the bath a little longer, then lifted out and swirled in air. The reading just after the jump sits below the true freezing point because some of the water is already ice. The reading when the last ice melts is the freezing point.", size=full]{labs/l-1791872911324/1792255759937-q687e-cooling-curve.jpg}

# Part 3 — Table salt

This part repeats the Part 1 procedure with the table salt solution in place of plain water.

**3.1** Rinse the sample jar and thermometer with water, then with about 5 mL of table salt solution, and discard the rinse.

**3.2** Pour table salt solution into the clean sample jar to a depth of about **2 cm** (about 15 mL). Place the thermometer in the liquid with its tip in the middle, about 1 cm above the bottom and away from the side of the jar.

**3.3** Push the sample jar down into the bath until the ice and brine come up to about the level of the liquid inside, and pack ice around it so it stays put. The rim of the jar must stay well above the bath so no brine gets in.

**3.4** Stir gently and continuously by moving the thermometer in small circles, keeping its tip in the middle of the liquid, and watch the reading fall. The sample cools below its freezing point without freezing. Then ice appears all at once and the reading jumps up by a degree or more within a few seconds. If the reading reaches −8.0 °C and there is still no ice, touch the corner of an ice cube to the surface of the liquid for about 1 s and take it away.

**3.5** As soon as the reading jumps, lift the jar out of the bath and hold it in the air. Keep swirling the thermometer through the slush. The reading rises slowly as the ice melts. If the jar holds only a trace of ice, put it back in the bath for 20 s and lift it out again.

**3.6** When only a few small pieces of ice are left, slow down. Swirl just enough to keep the liquid mixed and watch the ice. The **freezing point** is the reading at the moment the last piece of ice disappears. Record the **freezing point** to 0.1 °C in the Table salt row, Trial 1.

**3.7** Set the jar back in the bath as in step 3.3 and follow steps 3.4 through 3.6 again for Trial 2.

**3.8** Empty the jar.

# Part 4 — Epsom salt

This part repeats the Part 1 procedure with the Epsom salt solution in place of plain water.

**4.1** Rinse the sample jar and thermometer with water, then with about 5 mL of Epsom salt solution, and discard the rinse.

**4.2** Pour Epsom salt solution into the clean sample jar to a depth of about **2 cm** (about 15 mL). Place the thermometer in the liquid with its tip in the middle, about 1 cm above the bottom and away from the side of the jar.

**4.3** Push the sample jar down into the bath until the ice and brine come up to about the level of the liquid inside, and pack ice around it so it stays put. The rim of the jar must stay well above the bath so no brine gets in.

**4.4** Stir gently and continuously by moving the thermometer in small circles, keeping its tip in the middle of the liquid, and watch the reading fall. The sample cools below its freezing point without freezing. Then ice appears all at once and the reading jumps up by a degree or more within a few seconds. If the reading reaches −8.0 °C and there is still no ice, touch the corner of an ice cube to the surface of the liquid for about 1 s and take it away.

**4.5** As soon as the reading jumps, lift the jar out of the bath and hold it in the air. Keep swirling the thermometer through the slush. The reading rises slowly as the ice melts. If the jar holds only a trace of ice, put it back in the bath for 20 s and lift it out again.

**4.6** When only a few small pieces of ice are left, slow down. Swirl just enough to keep the liquid mixed and watch the ice. The **freezing point** is the reading at the moment the last piece of ice disappears. Record the **freezing point** to 0.1 °C in the Epsom salt row, Trial 1.

**4.7** Set the jar back in the bath as in step 4.3 and follow steps 4.4 through 4.6 again for Trial 2.

**4.8** Empty the jar.

Between trials, if the bath is mostly liquid or reads warmer than −8.0 °C, pour off some brine and top it up with ice and salt.

From the masses, calculate the molality of each solution. The ice-point reading from step 0.8 and the two water trials measure the same temperature by two different routes, so compare them. Take the mean of the two water trials as the freezing point of water and the mean of the two trials for each solution, and from those find each freezing-point depression and each van't Hoff factor. Then set each value beside two numbers: the count of particles a formula unit would give if it simply came apart in water, and the accepted value at your molality from the curve below.

# Reference values

## Accepted van't Hoff factors

\figure[caption="Apparent van't Hoff factor of sodium chloride (upper panel), magnesium sulfate and sucrose (lower panel) at the freezing point, against molality. Find your solution's molality on the horizontal axis and read the accepted value from the curve for your solute.", size=full]{labs/l-1791872911324/1792255768114-hjv5r-accepted-vant-hoff.png}

\info[label="About the accepted curves"]{
Each curve is the freezing-point depression divided by 1.86 °C·kg/mol and by the molality, the same arithmetic as for your own data. Molality on the horizontal axis is for the anhydrous solute per kilogram of total water. The sodium chloride and magnesium sulfate curves follow measured freezing points from the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, "Concentrative Properties of Aqueous Solutions" (data of Wolf, 1966), shown as markers. The sucrose curve is calculated from the water activity of sucrose solutions given by the Norrish equation with the constant of Chirife, Ferro Fontán and Benmergui (1980). Below about 0.2 mol/kg the tabulated magnesium sulfate freezing points are rounded too coarsely to pin down a curve, so none is drawn there.
}

# Data

Freezing-point depression constant of water: 1.86 °C·kg/mol. Molar masses: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ 342.30 g/mol; NaCl 58.44 g/mol; MgSO₄·7H₂O 246.47 g/mol; MgSO₄ 120.37 g/mol; H₂O 18.02 g/mol.

If you choose to sign in with Google, the site stores only your name and email address so your lab entries can follow you between devices. Your entries are visible to you and to the site admins. Nothing is sold or shared with anyone else, and no advertising is shown.

You can delete your account and every saved entry at any time from the account page. Anonymous usage statistics (which labs are opened, on what kind of device) are collected without any personal information.
